blocks.text: 1. Multi-Head Attention

blocks.alt: An input feeds three heads in parallel, which concatenate into one output

blocks.text: Cross-Attention, the previous topic, formalized attention between two genuinely different sequences. Multi-Head Attention runs several attention computations in parallel for richer representations, closing this module with a genuinely powerful synthesis.
It closes the Attention Mechanism module by combining every idea already covered throughout it, explored in complete depth throughout this final topic of the module.
2. Recapping Every Attention Variant

This connects back to every single Attention variant already covered throughout this entire module. Self-Attention, Cross-Attention, and Scaled Dot-Product Attention all compute genuinely just one single attention pattern at a time.
Multi-Head Attention genuinely runs several of these computations simultaneously instead, a genuinely powerful extension of every technique already covered throughout the rest of this module.
3. Why One Pattern Is Genuinely Not Enough

blocks.alt: A single attention head only captures one relationship pattern

blocks.text: A genuinely important motivating limitation connects back to Parallel filters, already covered in GoogLeNet. A genuinely single attention pattern can only genuinely capture one kind of relationship at a time.

This genuinely real limitation, already covered in this section, directly motivates the entire rest of this topic, echoing the exact same motivation already covered for GoogLeNet's own parallel filter design.
4. Multiple Heads, Explained

blocks.alt: One head focuses on syntax while another focuses on semantics

blocks.text: This connects back to why one pattern is not enough, already covered in this topic. Each genuinely separate attention head genuinely learns its own distinct Query, Key, and Value projections.
This lets different heads genuinely specialize in capturing genuinely different kinds of relationships, directly addressing the limitation already covered in the previous section.

blocks.text: 5. A Parallel Computation Benefit

blocks.alt: Head 1 and head 2 are both computed in parallel

blocks.text: This connects back to GoogLeNet's own Inception Module, already covered in the CNN Architectures module. Just like GoogLeNet ran several genuinely different filter sizes in parallel, already covered there.

Multi-Head Attention genuinely runs several genuinely different attention computations in parallel too, echoing the exact same parallel-branch design philosophy already covered for that earlier architecture.
6. Concatenating The Heads
This connects back to stacking feature maps, already covered in Feature Maps. Every single head's own output genuinely gets concatenated together into one combined result.
This is a genuinely direct parallel to the feature map stacking already covered throughout the CNN module, combining multiple genuinely separate computations into one unified representation.

blocks.content: This concatenation approach, already covered in this topic, directly mirrors the exact same stacking mechanism already covered throughout the entire CNN module, applied here to attention heads instead of convolutional filters.

blocks.text: 7. The Final Linear Projection

blocks.alt: Concatenated heads pass through a linear projection to produce the final output

blocks.text: A genuinely necessary final step connects back to fully connected layers, already covered in Network Architecture. A genuinely final linear layer combines that concatenated result back down to the expected output size.

This genuinely necessary step, already covered in this section, ensures the combined, concatenated output from every head, already covered in the previous section, matches the dimensions the rest of the network expects.
8. What Different Heads Genuinely Learn

This connects back to interpretability, already covered in Encoder-Decoder Attention. Different heads genuinely often learn to specialize, some genuinely attending to nearby words, others to genuinely distant, syntactically related ones.

This is a genuinely fascinating, real, empirical finding worth understanding, directly extending the interpretability benefit already covered in that earlier topic to this genuinely richer, multi-head setting.

blocks.text: 9. Recapping The Computational Cost
This connects back to a genuine computational cost consideration, already covered in Self-Attention. Multi-Head Attention genuinely costs somewhat more computation than a single attention head.

This is a genuinely real, honest tradeoff for the genuinely richer representational power already covered throughout this topic, echoing the same efficiency-versus-capability tension already covered generally throughout this course.
10. Recognizing Why Multi-Head Attention Is Genuinely The Standard Choice Today

blocks.alt: Building a modern transformer points toward multi-head attention

blocks.text: This connects forward to Transformers, covered later in this course, built almost entirely from this exact mechanism. Multi-Head Attention, already covered in this topic, is genuinely the single most important building block there.

Wanting genuinely richer, more nuanced representations than a single attention pattern allows is another genuine case where Multi-Head Attention, already covered, directly delivers exactly that richness.
11. Worked Example

The example below directly demonstrates computing Multi-Head Attention with several parallel heads, then concatenating and projecting their outputs, illustrating the concepts already covered throughout this topic.

code.content:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
sequence_length = 4
hidden_size = 8
num_heads = 2
head_size = hidden_size // num_heads  # already covered as multiple heads, explained in this topic

sequence = rng.normal(size=(sequence_length, hidden_size))

def softmax(x):
    exp_x = np.exp(x - np.max(x, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
    return exp_x / exp_x.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)

def attention_head(sequence, head_size, rng):
    W_query = rng.normal(size=(head_size, hidden_size)) * 0.1
    W_key = rng.normal(size=(head_size, hidden_size)) * 0.1
    W_value = rng.normal(size=(head_size, hidden_size)) * 0.1
    q, k, v = sequence @ W_query.T, sequence @ W_key.T, sequence @ W_value.T
    scores = q @ k.T / np.sqrt(head_size)
    weights = softmax(scores)
    return weights @ v

head_outputs = [attention_head(sequence, head_size, rng) for _ in range(num_heads)]  # already covered as a parallel computation benefit
concatenated = np.concatenate(head_outputs, axis=-1)  # already covered as concatenating the heads in this topic

W_output = rng.normal(size=(hidden_size, hidden_size)) * 0.1
final_output = concatenated @ W_output.T  # already covered as the final linear projection in this topic

print(f"Number of heads: {num_heads}, each producing shape: {head_outputs[0].shape}")
print(f"Concatenated shape: {concatenated.shape}")
print(f"Final output shape (already covered as the final linear projection in this topic): {final_output.shape}")

blocks.text: 12. Attention Mechanism: Module Complete

items: Multi-Head Attention runs several attention computations in parallel for richer representations.
A single attention pattern can only capture one kind of relationship at a time.
Each head learns its own distinct Query, Key, and Value projections.
This parallels GoogLeNet's own Inception Module, running several computations in parallel.
Every head's output gets concatenated together into one combined result.
A final linear layer projects that concatenated result back to the expected output size.
Different heads often specialize, some attending to nearby words, others to distant, related ones.
It costs somewhat more computation than a single head, a real, honest tradeoff for richer power.

This completes the Attention Mechanism module: Why Attention, Encoder-Decoder Attention, Query, Key, and Value, Dot-Product, Scaled Dot-Product, and Additive Attention, Self-Attention, Cross-Attention, and Multi-Head Attention.
